pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Types of Chemical Reaction

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Chemistry, Chemical reactions):** pupils are taught "combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions" and to represent chemical reactions using formulae and word equations, building on the idea that a chemical reaction rearranges atoms to form new substances while conserving mass.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-PS1-2):** analyse [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS1-2] they interact to determine whether a chemical reaction has occurred — the four types are recognised by their characteristic evidence.

- **Operational details:** Give pupils a small toolkit of four named reaction patterns so they can classify what they observe: combustion (burning a fuel in oxygen, releasing heat/light — e.g. methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water); oxidation (a substance gains oxygen — e.g. magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide, and rusting as slow oxidation); thermal decomposition (heat breaks ONE compound into simpler substances — e.g. copper carbonate → copper oxide + carbon dioxide); and displacement (a more reactive element takes another's place — iron + copper sulfate → iron sulfate + copper). The key skill is sorting a reaction into the right family from its evidence: is a fuel burning? is oxygen being gained? is one substance splitting apart on heating? is one element swapping for another? Represent each with a word equation and check atoms are conserved.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). Given a described or observed reaction, the child classifies it as combustion, oxidation, thermal decomposition or displacement and justifies the choice from the evidence and the word equation.
bestPractices: Give the four types as a classification toolkit and repeatedly practise sorting NEW reactions into them from evidence, rather than defining them once in isolation.

Anchor each type to a memorable observable signature — heat+light for combustion, a gained oxide for oxidation, a compound splitting on heating for thermal decomposition, a deposited metal for displacement.
Use word equations for every example and check atoms are conserved, reinforcing that reactions rearrange rather than create or destroy matter.
Surface overlap explicitly (magnesium burning is both combustion and oxidation) so pupils reason from evidence rather than assuming the categories are mutually exclusive.
Contrast thermal decomposition (one reactant → several products) with combination/oxidation (several → one) so the direction of change is clear.
keyRepresentations: A 2×2 grid of the four reaction types, each with a canonical word equation and its tell-tale evidence.
Word equations such as methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water, and copper carbonate → copper oxide + carbon dioxide.
The limewater test as the signature for CO2 released in thermal decomposition.
A displacement pairing (iron + copper sulfate) showing the deposited metal and colour change.
Before/after mass bars illustrating conservation of mass across each reaction type.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming the four categories are mutually exclusive, when e.g. burning magnesium is both combustion and oxidation.
Confusing thermal decomposition (heat splits one substance apart) with reactions that combine substances, or thinking heating always causes decomposition.
Thinking oxidation only means rusting, missing that any gain of oxygen (including vigorous burning) is oxidation.
Believing combustion 'destroys' matter because the fuel seems to disappear, rather than forming gaseous products of equal mass.
Treating displacement as any two substances swapping, ignoring that the more reactive element must displace the less reactive one.

learn.summary: Pupils aged 12–13 learn to classify chemical reactions into four families — combustion (burning a fuel in oxygen, releasing heat/light), oxidation (a substance gains oxygen, including rusting), thermal decomposition (heat breaks one compound into simpler substances), and displacement (a more reactive element takes another's place) — by reasoning from observable evidence and word equations, while checking that atoms (and therefore total mass) are conserved. The core skill is sorting NEW reactions into the right family from evidence, recognising that categories can overlap (burning magnesium is both combustion and oxidation).

activities.title: Name that reaction: sort by evidence
feedback: When magnesium burning is sorted as combustion, confirm it AND prompt: it also gains oxygen to form magnesium oxide, so it is oxidation too — the categories are not mutually exclusive.

If a reaction is sorted only by surface appearance, redirect to the defining evidence: is a fuel burning? is oxygen being gained? is ONE substance splitting on heating? is one element replacing another?
For copper carbonate -> copper oxide + carbon dioxide, name why it is thermal decomposition: heat breaks one compound into simpler substances (watch for the released gas and colour change).
activities.rationale: The target skill is classification from evidence, so repeated sorting of varied, novel reactions — and explicitly surfacing overlap — is intended to build evidence-based reasoning rather than rote category labels. Standards specify these four named reaction types and classifying substances by before/after evidence.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils are taught combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions, and to represent chemical reactions using formulae and word equations.
Analyse [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS1-2] they interact to determine whether a chemical reaction has occurred.
learnerActions: Take a shuffled set of reactions, some presented as word equations (e.g. copper carbonate -> copper oxide + carbon dioxide) and some as one-line observed scenes (e.g. a strip of magnesium flares white and leaves a powder; a piece of iron dipped in blue copper sulfate becomes coated with pink-brown metal).
Sort each reaction into one of four families: combustion, oxidation, thermal decomposition, displacement.
For each card, state the evidence that justifies your choice: heat and light, a gained oxide, one substance splitting apart on heating, or one element swapping for another.
Flag any reaction that seems to belong in two families and explain why (e.g. magnesium burning).
activities.intendedInsight: Each reaction family has a tell-tale observable signature, and you classify by reasoning from that evidence rather than by memorising definitions in isolation; some reactions legitimately belong to more than one family.

activities.title: Complete the word equation and check conservation
feedback: If a learner expects burning magnesium to lose mass, track the oxygen: magnesium + oxygen -> magnesium oxide, so the solid oxide is HEAVIER because oxygen from the air was added — while total mass (metal + oxygen) is unchanged.
For a reaction where the solid appears to lose mass (e.g. wood burning), point out the lost mass has left as gases — total mass is still conserved once the escaping gases are counted.
If the atom check is skipped, prompt the learner to list the elements on each side before deciding the equation is complete.
activities.rationale: Using word equations and an atom/mass check for every example reinforces conservation of mass and counters the idea that combustion destroys matter. This connects the classification skill to the underlying representation of reactions required by the standards.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils are taught combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions, and to represent chemical reactions using formulae and word equations.
learnerActions: Complete word equations with missing reactants or products, e.g. methane + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water, and copper carbonate -> copper oxide + carbon dioxide.

After writing each equation, check that every element present before the reaction also appears after it. A word equation shows which elements are present, not how many atoms of each, so this check is consistent with atoms being neither created nor destroyed but does not prove it on its own.

Draw or compare before/after mass bars and explain that the TOTAL mass stays the same because atoms are only rearranged; then note that the solid you can actually weigh may appear to gain mass (magnesium takes in oxygen from the air) or lose mass (wood releases gases) depending on whether gas is absorbed or given off.
Match each reaction to its tell-tale sign: heat+light, gains oxygen, one substance splits into two or more simpler substances on heating, an element swapped out.
activities.intendedInsight: Reactions rearrange atoms rather than create or destroy matter, so total mass is conserved even when the weighable solid appears to change; word equations and the atom check make this explicit for every reaction type.

activities.title: Reaction bench: observe the signatures before sorting
feedback: When the carbonate is heated, point to the limewater turning cloudy as the signature that carbon dioxide was released — evidence of thermal decomposition.
For the displacement station, highlight the deposited metal and solution colour change, and connect it to the more reactive element replacing the less reactive one.

If a learner misreads heating a carbonate as melting, contrast melting (same substance, reversible) with decomposition (new substances form, here a gas is released, and often there is a colour change, e.g. green copper carbonate turning to black copper oxide).
activities.rationale: Observing each reaction's signature before abstract sorting may make the categories concrete and is intended to support evidence-based classification; this is a proposed scaffold, not a verified requirement. The limewater test and displacement colour change are concrete, optional interaction examples. Note: auto-written equations and the limewater cue are illustrative scaffolds, not the only route to the concept.
learnerActions: Visit four stations that each trigger one reaction type: light a fuel (combustion, heat and light), heat a metal in oxygen (oxidation, an oxide forms), heat a carbonate so the released gas turns limewater cloudy (thermal decomposition, CO2 detected), and dip a metal into a solution of a salt of a less reactive metal, e.g. iron into copper sulfate (displacement, a metal deposits with a colour change).
Watch each reaction auto-produce its word equation and note the observable signature.
Switch to a 'name that reaction' mode where the label is hidden and classify each reaction from its evidence alone.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing each reaction type and its signature (flame, oxide layer, gas released on heating, deposited metal) is intended to build perceptual hooks that later classification can draw on.

activities.title: Predict–Observe–Explain: weighing burning magnesium
feedback: If the learner predicts the powder weighs less, revisit: metal + oxygen -> metal oxide means oxygen is added, so the solid mass INCREASES while total mass is unchanged.
If oxidation is thought to mean only rusting, group burning, rusting, and magnesium-burning together: all are gaining oxygen, with rusting the slow case and burning the fast case.
For the wood comparison, note the escaping gases carry away the 'lost' mass — total mass is still conserved once gases are counted.
activities.rationale: The counter-intuitive solid-mass gain discriminates learners who understand combustion as combining with oxygen from those holding a 'burning destroys matter' model; the pre-observation reasoning is the diagnostic part. This directly supports the conservation and oxidation evidence in the objective.
sourceClaims: Analyse [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS1-2] they interact to determine whether a chemical reaction has occurred.
learnerActions: Before burning, weigh a coil of magnesium ribbon and predict whether the mass of the white powder afterwards will be more, less, or the same — and state WHY.

Heat the ribbon in a crucible with a lid, lifting the lid slightly now and then to let air in while keeping the white smoke in. Then weigh the crucible, lid and product and compare with the crucible, lid and ribbon before heating.
Compare your prediction with the result and explain what combustion/oxidation actually did to the magnesium.
Reconcile this with wood burning, which leaves only light ash: where did the wood's mass go?
activities.intendedInsight: Combustion of magnesium is oxidation: the metal combines with oxygen from the air, so the solid product gains mass. Burning does not destroy matter; where mass seems to be lost (wood, candle) it has escaped as gases, so total matter is conserved.

activities.title: Complete vs incomplete combustion
feedback: If a learner treats all burning as producing only CO2 and water, point to soot and carbon monoxide as evidence of incomplete combustion when oxygen is limited.
Reinforce that both complete and incomplete combustion are still combustion — the fuel burns in oxygen — they differ in how much oxygen is available and therefore in the products.
activities.rationale: The objective's evidence list requires distinguishing complete from incomplete combustion; contrasting the two product sets from observable clues builds that distinction, and combustion is explicitly listed in the KS3 content.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils are taught combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions, and to represent chemical reactions using formulae and word equations.
learnerActions: Compare complete combustion of a hydrocarbon fuel such as methane or candle wax (products carbon dioxide and water) with its incomplete combustion (products including carbon monoxide and soot).
Identify, from described evidence such as soot deposits or a smoky yellow flame, whether combustion was complete or incomplete.
Explain why limited oxygen leads to incomplete combustion and the formation of soot and carbon monoxide.
activities.intendedInsight: Combustion is not a single outcome: the amount of available oxygen changes the products, distinguishing clean complete combustion from sooty incomplete combustion.

constraints: Drag-to-bin sorting, multiple-choice and matching tasks can assess and rehearse classification, but a selection/recognition response does not by itself require a learner to construct an original word equation or explanation; include fill-in and explain-why tasks where independent production is the goal.

A tappable four-panel reference grid of the four reaction types is useful for vocabulary and definitions but, being a fixed reveal, does not itself give practice classifying new, unseen reactions — pair it with sorting activities.
Surface overlap explicitly: the four families are NOT mutually exclusive (burning magnesium is both combustion and oxidation); do not teach them as rigid disjoint boxes.
Distinguish thermal decomposition (one reactant -> several products on heating) from melting (same substance, reversible, no new substance) and from combination reactions (several -> one).
When discussing conservation of mass, always account for gases taken in or released: total mass is conserved even when the weighable solid appears to gain mass (magnesium) or lose mass (wood).

Any physical enactment in these activities — the reaction-bench stations AND the magnesium Predict–Observe–Explain burn — involves real flames, heating and chemicals; burning magnesium in particular emits intense bright light that must not be viewed directly, so all such tasks require appropriate supervision, eye protection and safety provision.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified, and all activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source labels the NGSS MS-PS1-2 claim as verified:false; treat the standards alignment to that source, and its use as support for evidence-based classification, as unconfirmed.

The original marked the 3D and conversation formats as 'poor' with reasoning such as '3D adds cost without insight' and 'open dialogue... does not deliver the sort-by-evidence practice'. These are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws; they have been softened/omitted. Dialogue or spatial models are simply different, non-essential affordances here.

The original claimed 'static reveals cannot exercise the classification-from-new-evidence skill'. Reworded to the narrower, accurate point that a fixed reference grid does not itself provide new-reaction sorting practice; a fixed example can still teach.

The reaction-bench activity's claim that enacting signatures 'builds the perceptual hooks' for classification is an untested efficacy assertion; its sourceClaims were set to [] because the available source claim supports only the curriculum content, not the pedagogical ordering, and the rationale/insight were qualified as intended/proposed.

The before/after mass-bar prompt was reworded to avoid implying TOTAL mass can go up or down: total mass is conserved, while the observable solid may appear to gain mass (Mg absorbs oxygen) or lose mass (wood releases gases).

Checking atom conservation from word equations alone confirms which elements appear on each side but not numeric atom counts (that needs formulae); this reflects the original framing and is retained as an approximation.
Safety: the magnesium POE burn was previously covered by no explicit safety note; the safety constraint was broadened to include it, flagging the bright-light hazard of burning magnesium.

Self-audit of chemistry: magnesium + oxygen -> magnesium oxide genuinely increases the solid mass (oxygen added); wood burning appears to lose mass because gaseous products escape — both consistent with conservation of total mass. Copper carbonate -> copper oxide + carbon dioxide is a valid thermal decomposition. No arithmetic or force/motion claims required correction.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain: weigh a coil of magnesium ribbon, then burn it in a crucible and weigh the white oxide. Ask the child to predict whether the mass goes up, down, or stays the same, and WHY, before burning. A 'burning destroys matter' model predicts a decrease. The oxide is heavier (oxygen added). The pre-observation reasoning is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: Wood burning leaves light ash — but magnesium gains mass. Are these really both combustion? Where did the wood's mass go?
How is complete combustion (CO₂ + water) different from incomplete combustion, and why does incomplete give soot and carbon monoxide?
Why is rusting called oxidation as well as burning? What do they share?
Heating copper carbonate turns it black and gives off a gas. Melting or a reaction — how do you know?
assess.correctAnswer: The white powder weighs MORE than the ribbon. Combustion here is oxidation: the magnesium GAINS oxygen from the air, combining with it to form magnesium oxide — so the added oxygen adds mass. Burning doesn't destroy matter; it combines the fuel with oxygen. Full marks explain the mass increase by oxygen being added, not by anything being 'used up'.

errorPatterns.pattern: burning destroys matter, so products always weigh less ('it burns away')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Track the oxygen: metal + oxygen → metal oxide, so mass increases. Where fumes escape (wood, candle) the lost mass leaves as gases — still conserved. Weigh magnesium before/after.
errorPatterns.distractor: Less — burning always destroys some of the material.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: predicts the oxide weighs less than the metal; explains combustion as disappearance

errorPatterns.pattern: oxidation only means rusting ('oxidation is when iron goes rusty, nothing else')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Oxidation = gaining oxygen, of which rusting is the slow case and combustion the fast case. Group burning, rusting and magnesium-burning as oxidation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: restricts oxidation to rust; doesn't see burning or magnesium+oxygen as oxidation

errorPatterns.pattern: thermal decomposition is just melting ('heating it made it melt, not break apart')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast melting (same substance, reversible) with thermal decomposition (heat breaks ONE compound into new substances, e.g. copper carbonate → copper oxide + CO₂, colour change, gas). Use the signs of a new substance.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: reads heating a carbonate (which breaks into oxide + CO₂) as a physical melt rather than a reaction making new substances

responseLevels.gap: Predicts mass loss on burning; equates oxidation only with rust; reads decomposition as melting.
responseLevels.full: Explains combustion/oxidation as combining with oxygen (mass added; wood's loss leaves as gas), classifies all four reaction types from equations, distinguishes complete from incomplete combustion, and separates thermal decomposition from melting by the new-substance test.
responseLevels.partial: Identifies the four reaction types and predicts the magnesium mass gain, but can't reconcile it with wood losing mass (escaping gas) or distinguish complete/incomplete combustion — recognises types without the unifying conservation reasoning.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I burn a coil of magnesium ribbon in air and it leaves a white powder (magnesium oxide). A student says 'burning always destroys stuff, so the white powder must weigh LESS than the ribbon.' Would the powder weigh less, more, or the same — and the important part, explain what combustion/oxidation actually does to the magnesium.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-two reason distinguishes a child who understands combustion/oxidation as COMBINING WITH OXYGEN (mass added, atoms rearranged) from one who thinks burning destroys or lightens matter. The counter-intuitive mass gain is the discriminator — the 'burning = loss' model predicts the wrong direction.
